name: South Carolina State University
formerNames: Colored Normal Industrial Agricultural and Mechanical College of South Carolina
description: Created by the South Carolina General Assembly in 1896, separating the state's Black land-grant program from Claflin, where it had operated since 1872. SC State is the state's only public 4-year HBCU and the alma mater of Congressman Jim Clyburn and media owner Armstrong Williams. In 1968 it was the site of the Orangeburg massacre.

facts.d: The South Carolina Agricultural and Mechanical Institute began within Claflin College in 1872 before the 1896 act of separation.
On February 8, 1968, state police killed three students and wounded 27 during a protest against a segregated bowling alley.
Hall of Famers Deacon Jones, Harry Carson and Donnie Shell played at SC State.

name: Claflin University
affiliation: Methodist Episcopal Church (now United Methodist Church); UNCF
description: Founded in 1869 by Methodist Episcopal minister Alonzo Webster to educate freedmen, and named for Massachusetts governor William Claflin and his father Lee Claflin, a Boston philanthropist. South Carolina's oldest HBCU; its alumni include realtor-legislator Earl M. Middleton and photographer Cecil J. Williams.

facts.d: Opened October 27, 1869, as a school for freedmen and their children.
A 2020 gift of $20 million from MacKenzie Scott was the largest single gift in its history.

connections.label: founded by Methodist Episcopal minister Alonzo Webster

name: Benedict College
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society; American Baptist Churches USA; UNCF
description: Opened in 1870 as Benedict Institute after Bathsheba A. Benedict of Rhode Island, representing the American Baptist Home Mission Society, gave $13,000 for land. Chartered as a college in 1894. Alumni include civil rights leaders Modjeska Monteith Simkins and Septima Clark, funeral-home owner I. S. Leevy Johnson and KFC executive Walt Simon.

facts.d: Bathsheba Benedict's $13,000 bought the land; Rev. Timothy Dodge was the first teacher and president.
Benedict Institute became Benedict College on November 2, 1894.

name: Allen University
description: Founded in 1870 in Cokesbury, South Carolina, as Payne Institute by AME ministers including John M. Brown; moved to Columbia and renamed for AME founder Richard Allen in 1880. Alumni include Rev. Clementa C. Pinckney and Briggs v. Elliott organizer Rev. Joseph A. DeLaine.

facts.d: Payne Institute relocated in 1880 and took Richard Allen's name.
The Allen University Historic District was listed on the National Register in 1975.

name: Morris College
affiliation: Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of South Carolina; UNCF
description: Founded in 1908 by the Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of South Carolina (organized by Jacob J. Durham), which still owns and operates it. Named for Black community leader Frank Morris; it began as a grade school, high school and college and awarded its first bachelor's degree in 1915.

facts.d: Founded and operated by South Carolina's Black Baptist convention.
Luns C. Richardson led the college from 1974 to 2017.

connections.label: founded by the Baptist Educational and Missionary Convention of SC

name: Voorhees University
formerNames: Voorhees Industrial Institute for Colored Youths
description: Founded in 1897 by Tuskegee-trained educator Elizabeth Evelyn Wright as the Denmark Industrial School; New Jersey philanthropist Ralph Voorhees gave $5,000 in 1902 for land and buildings. Affiliated with the Episcopal Church since 1924 and renamed a university in 2022.

facts.d: Elizabeth Evelyn Wright opened the school on April 14, 1897, modeled on Tuskegee.
Became Voorhees University in 2022, its 125th anniversary year.

name: Clinton College
kind: Private HBCU · AME Zion Christian college
description: Founded in 1894 as Clinton Institute and named for AME Zion Bishop Caleb Isom Clinton of the Palmetto Conference. It became a junior college in 1965 and a four-year college in 2013; it is a very small institution that reported severe cash-flow problems in 2026.

facts.d: Gained accreditation as a four-year institution in 2013 (TRACS).
Reportedly missed employee paychecks and insurance payments in April 2026.

name: Denmark Technical College
formerNames: Denmark Branch of the South Carolina Trade School System
description: Authorized by the South Carolina General Assembly in 1947 and opened in 1948 as a trade school for Black students, teaching tailoring, cosmetology, building trades and auto mechanics. Its motto was "He Who Hath a Trade Hath an Estate." Comedian J. Anthony Brown trained there as a tailor.

facts.d: Opened March 1, 1948, under founding principal Lorry H. Dawkins.
Became Denmark Technical College on gaining SACS accreditation.

name: Friendship College
fate: Closed permanently in 1981 and its buildings were later demolished after a fire.
description: A Baptist school founded in 1891 by Masel Phillip Hall in Rock Hill. Its students formed the Friendship Nine, who in 1961 chose jail over bail after a lunch-counter sit-in, inspiring the "jail, no bail" strategy. NBA champion Harthorne Wingo attended.

facts.d: The 1961 Rock Hill sit-in by Friendship students is commemorated as the Friendship Nine.
The college closed permanently in December 1981.

name: Avery Normal Institute
fate: Closed by the Charleston County school board in 1954 after Brown v. Board; students merged into Burke High School. The Avery Research Center (College of Charleston) now occupies the building.
description: Founded in Charleston in 1865 by the American Missionary Association, Avery trained generations of Black teachers and leaders, among them Septima Clark and NAACP pioneer Edwin Harleston. After it closed, alumni founded the Avery Institute of Afro-American History and Culture, which led to today's Avery Research Center.

facts.d: Avery's normal course prepared Black teachers for South Carolina schools.
The Avery Research Center opened in the building in 1990.

name: Florida A&M University
affiliation: State University System of Florida; 1890 land-grant
formerNames: State Normal College for Colored Students
State Normal and Industrial College for Colored Students
Florida Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes
description: Founded October 3, 1887, as the State Normal College for Colored Students. FAMU's School of Business and Industry, built by founding dean Sybil Collins Mobley, is a major pipeline of corporate executives, among them Microsoft chairman John W. Thompson, Helen of Troy CEO Scott Uzzell, Independence Blue Cross CEO Gregory Deavens and Northern Trust leaders Shundrawn Thomas and Lyle Logan.

facts.d: Founding dean Sybil Mobley sat on the boards of Anheuser-Busch, Sears, Hershey and others and built an executive-style business school.
SBI's Big Board, begun in 1983, honors donors of at least $100,000 each in endowed scholarships.
Florida A&M College for Negroes became Florida Agricultural and Mechanical University in 1953.

name: Bethune-Cookman University
formerNames: Daytona Educational and Industrial Training School for Negro Girls
Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute for Girls
description: Founded in 1904 by Mary McLeod Bethune as a school for Black girls in a rented house in Daytona; it merged with Jacksonville's Cookman Institute for boys (1872) in 1923. Bethune was also an insurance founder and investor, and the school's alumni include Harry T. Moore and Madam C. J. Walker executive Marjorie Joyner.

facts.d: Bethune opened the school in 1904 with six students and 50-cent tuition.
Joined with Cookman Institute in 1923 (name Daytona Cookman Collegiate Institute by 1927); Bethune-Cookman College from 1941, university from 2007.

name: Cookman Institute
fate: Merged with Mary McLeod Bethune's Daytona school in 1923 to form what became Bethune-Cookman University.
description: Founded in Jacksonville in 1872 by Rev. D. S. Darnell under Methodist sponsorship, Cookman was one of Florida's first institutions of higher learning for Black students. A. Philip Randolph graduated as valedictorian in 1907; Florida's first Black judge, James Dean, also attended.

facts.d: A. Philip Randolph was valedictorian of Cookman's 1907 class.
Combined with the Daytona Normal and Industrial Institute.

name: Edward Waters University
formerNames: East Florida Scientific and Divinity High School
description: Florida's first independent institution of higher education and first HBCU, founded in 1866 by members of the AME Church in Jacksonville. Renamed for AME bishop Edward Waters in 1892, it became a university in 2021. Negro leagues great Buck O'Neil finished high school and two years of college there.

facts.d: Founded 1866, the year after the Civil War ended.
Centennial Hall (1916) is on the National Register of Historic Places.

name: Florida Memorial University
formerNames: Florida Normal and Industrial Memorial College
description: Traces to the Florida Baptist Institute (Live Oak, 1879) and the Florida Baptist Academy (Jacksonville, later St. Augustine), which combined and moved to Miami Gardens. James Weldon and J. Rosamond Johnson wrote "Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing" there in 1900. Alumni include aviator Barrington Irving and civil rights martyr Harry T. Moore.

facts.d: "Lift Ev'ry Voice and Sing" was written in 1900 by the Johnson brothers; Rosamond taught at the school.
The Live Oak and St. Augustine institutions merged in 1941; university status in 2006.

name: University of the Virgin Islands
affiliation: Government of the U.S. Virgin Islands; land-grant
description: Founded in 1962 as the College of the Virgin Islands and designated an HBCU in 1986, when it took its current name. UVI has educated much of the Caribbean's political leadership, including USVI Governor Albert Bryan Jr. (MBA) and Sint Maarten Prime Minister Silveria Jacobs.

facts.d: The only HBCU outside the continental U.S.; designated in 1986.
Alumni include heads of government and ministers across the Eastern Caribbean.

sources.label: Wikipedia — University of the Virgin Islands

name: Booker T. Washington Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Nominally merged with Pensacola Junior College in 1965.
description: The first of Florida's twelve public Black junior colleges, opened in Pensacola in 1949. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1949–1965.

name: Carver Junior College
kind: Public HBCU · Florida Black junior college (defunct)
fate: Closed in 1963, among the first of the Black junior colleges to shut as Florida desegregated.
description: One of the eleven Black junior colleges Florida opened after Brown v. Board of Education to sustain "separate but equal." Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

facts.d: Florida built twelve Black public junior colleges between 1949 and 1961 to forestall integration.
Operated 1960–1963.

fate: Closed in 1964 as Florida desegregated its junior colleges.

description: Opened in 1957 by the Pinellas County Board of Public Instruction for Black students, first in Gibbs High School's building; it was regionally accredited. Like the rest of the system, it was shut down once desegregation followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

name: John W. Thompson
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published net-worth figure found; based on years of senior public-company or large-enterprise executive compensation. Includes a decade as Symantec CEO and a minority Warriors stake.
hbcuStory: Earned a BBA from Florida A&M in 1971 (later an MIT Sloan MBA, 1983). FAMU's School of Business and Industry inducted him into its Hall of Fame in 2010.
humbleBeginnings: Born at Fort Dix, New Jersey, and raised in Florida, he attended John F. Kennedy High School in Riviera Beach before FAMU.
breakthrough: Spent 28 years at IBM (1971–1999), rising to general manager of IBM Americas, then became CEO of Symantec in 1999 and ran it for a decade.
legacy: Became the first Black chairman of Microsoft (2014–2021), presiding over the board that picked Satya Nadella as CEO, and joined the investor group behind the Golden State Warriors.

breakthroughDetail.d: Left IBM as GM of IBM Americas to take Symantec's CEO job in 1999; retired April 2009.
Joined Microsoft's board in 2012 and chaired it from February 2014 to June 2021.
Later served as CEO of Virtual Instruments, leaving after its 2016 merger with Load DynamiX.

legacyDetail.d: Listed as a part owner of the Golden State Warriors.
Black Enterprise lists him among top HBCU-educated executives.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Black executives who attended HBCUs

connections.label: sales to GM of IBM Americas, 1971–1999

name: G. Scott Uzzell
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published net-worth figure found; based on years of senior public-company or large-enterprise executive compensation.
base: El Paso, TX (Helen of Troy HQ)
hbcuStory: Holds a bachelor's degree in business from Florida A&M's School of Business and Industry (MBA, University of Chicago); he serves on the FAMU Foundation board.
humbleBeginnings: Built his career in beverage brand management at The Coca-Cola Company, rising to president of its Venturing & Emerging Brands group.
breakthrough: Nike named him president and CEO of Converse in January 2019; he later ran Nike's North America operating unit (2023–2024).
legacy: In September 2025 he became CEO of Helen of Troy, the Nasdaq-listed maker of OXO, Hydro Flask and Revlon-licensed appliances.

breakthroughDetail.d: Led Coca-Cola's Venturing & Emerging Brands unit, which invested in new beverage brands.
Ran Converse for Nike from 2019 to 2023.
Appointed CEO effective September 1, 2025.

legacyDetail.d: Serves on the FAMU Foundation board; named to Savoy's list of influential Black executives.

name: Gregory E. Deavens
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published net-worth figure found; based on years of senior public-company or large-enterprise executive compensation.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in accounting from Florida A&M's School of Business and Industry and became a CPA.
humbleBeginnings: Began his career in public accounting at Price Waterhouse, then held finance roles at GE Capital, Cigna, New York Life and MassMutual.
breakthrough: Joined Independence Blue Cross in 2017 as EVP, CFO and treasurer and became president and CEO in January 2021.
legacy: The first African American to lead Independence, one of the largest health insurers in the Philadelphia region.

breakthroughDetail.d: CFO and treasurer of Independence Blue Cross from 2017.
Named president and CEO of Independence Health Group in 2021, a first for an African American.

legacyDetail.d: Profiled by AHIP, the national health-insurance trade association, among industry leaders.

sources.label: Philadelphia Tribune — Deavens named first African American leader of IBX

name: Shundrawn Thomas
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published net-worth figure found; based on years of senior public-company or large-enterprise executive compensation.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in accounting from Florida A&M (MBA, University of Chicago Booth); inducted into the FAMU SBI Hall of Fame in 2014.
humbleBeginnings: Rose through Northern Trust's investment business after starting in finance out of FAMU.
breakthrough: Became president of Northern Trust Asset Management, a member of the firm's executive group overseeing roughly $1.3 trillion in assets.
legacy: Left to found The Copia Group, a private investment firm providing capital to lower-middle-market companies; he sits on the board of Reinsurance Group of America.

breakthroughDetail.d: Led Northern Trust Asset Management and sat on Northern Trust's executive management group.
Founded and is managing partner of The Copia Group.

legacyDetail.d: Director of Reinsurance Group of America; also on the FAMU Foundation board.

name: Lyle Logan
wealthNote: Estimate only: no published net-worth figure found; based on years of senior public-company or large-enterprise executive compensation.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in accounting and economics from Florida A&M (MBA in finance, University of Chicago); in the inaugural FAMU SBI Hall of Fame class.
humbleBeginnings: Started in Chicago banking at Continental Bank (later Bank of America).
breakthrough: Joined Northern Trust in 2000, leading Chicago private banking, institutional sales, and the global financial institutions group, and rose to vice chairman.
legacy: Serves on boards including Heidrick & Struggles, Impax Asset Management Group plc (from 2024) and the National Geographic Society.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rose from EVP and managing director to vice chairman of Northern Trust.
Non-executive director of Impax Asset Management Group plc from May 2024.

legacyDetail.d: Lurie Children's Hospital, The Field Foundation and Chamberlain University boards.

sources.label: Impax — Lyle Logan appointed to board
DeVry Inc. 2012 proxy statement — director bio (age 53) (SEC)

name: Bernard Kinsey
hbcuStory: Graduated from Florida A&M in 1967, where he met his wife Shirley (FAMU English, 1967); later earned a Pepperdine MBA and received an honorary doctorate from FAMU.
humbleBeginnings: Born in West Palm Beach; after FAMU he was hired as the first Black sales representative at Humble Oil.
breakthrough: Spent about two decades at Xerox, becoming a vice president, then co-chaired and served as COO of Rebuild L.A. after the 1992 uprising.
legacy: With Shirley he built the Kinsey Collection, one of the largest private collections of African American art and history, which has toured nationally.

breakthroughDetail.d: Rose to vice president during a roughly 20-year Xerox career.
Co-chairman and COO of Rebuild L.A. under Peter Ueberroth, recruiting private investment after the 1992 unrest.

legacyDetail.d: Family-owned collection spanning 1632 to the present, now run by son Khalil.
Returned as a 2025 FAMU commencement speaker.

name: Will Packer
wealthNote: Estimate only: no authoritative published figure; based on producer fees and equity across a $1B+ box-office slate.
hbcuStory: Graduated magna cum laude from Florida A&M with a B.S. in electrical engineering in 1996; he and classmate Rob Hardy made their first film, Chocolate City, while students. FAMU named its amphitheater for him in 2021.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in St. Petersburg, Florida, and entered FAMU in 1991 as an engineering student.
breakthrough: Co-founded Rainforest Films with Rob Hardy, then launched Will Packer Productions in 2013 with Universal film and TV deals.
legacy: His films, including Think Like a Man, Ride Along and Girls Trip, have grossed more than $1 billion worldwide, with ten opening at No. 1.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built an independent Black film company with Rob Hardy before scaling to studio releases (dissolved 2014).
2013 deals with Universal Pictures and Universal Television.
Earned about $140 million on a $19 million budget in 2017.

legacyDetail.d: Will Packer Amphitheater and FAMU's Meritorious Achievement Award (2021).

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Black executives who attended HBCUs

name: Rob Hardy
hbcuStory: Attended Florida A&M, where he won the Bernard Hendricks Student Leadership Award and made Chocolate City (1994) with Will Packer.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Philadelphia; graduated from the George School in 1991 before FAMU.
breakthrough: Co-founded Rainforest Films, writing and directing Trois (2000), Trois 2 and The Gospel (2005) and executive-producing Stomp the Yard and Think Like a Man.
legacy: After Rainforest dissolved in 2014 he launched Rainforest Entertainment (2015), continuing to develop Black-led film and TV.

breakthroughDetail.d: Directed Trois (2000), an early theatrical release for Rainforest.
Wrote and directed The Gospel (2005).

legacyDetail.d: Founded in March 2015.

hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in broadcast journalism from Florida A&M in 1984 and later taught at the university.
humbleBeginnings: Built a career as a local and network news producer before joining CBS News in 2007.
breakthrough: Rose to executive vice president of CBS News, then was named president of ABC News in April 2021.
legacy: The first Black woman to lead a major U.S. broadcast network news division; she stepped down in 2024.

breakthroughDetail.d: Senior broadcast producer of CBS Evening News, then EVP of News.
Led ABC News from 2021 to 2024.

legacyDetail.d: First Black executive to run a major broadcast network news division.

name: Arian Simone
hbcuStory: Earned her bachelor's and MBA at Florida A&M (entering class of 1999); inducted onto the SBI Big Board in 2024 and endowed an SBI scholarship.
humbleBeginnings: Has described experiencing homelessness while building her first businesses before turning to venture investing.
breakthrough: Co-founded the Fearless Fund with fellow FAMU alumna Ayana Parsons, a VC fund for women-of-color founders backed by PayPal, Bank of America and Costco.
legacy: The FAMU Foundation invested in the fund in 2021, its first investment in a Black-led VC firm; the fund drew a high-profile 2023 legal challenge to its grant program.

breakthroughDetail.d: Pre-seed to Series A investor in women-of-color-led companies.
Backers include PayPal, Bank of America, Invest Atlanta and Costco.

legacyDetail.d: FAMU Foundation became an LP in 2021.
Endowed the Arian Simone Fearless Fund scholarship at SBI.

hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in accounting from Florida A&M in 1982 (honorary doctorate 2009); in 2001 he became the first chairman of FAMU's Board of Trustees. Inaugural SBI Hall of Fame inductee.
humbleBeginnings: Began his career as an IBM systems engineer in 1982 and later served as deputy receiver at the Florida Department of Insurance.
breakthrough: Founded Public Private Partnership, Inc., a Tallahassee strategic-planning and political consulting firm, in 1989.
legacy: Co-founded theGROUP in Washington in 2011 and has served on the boards of RLJ Lodging Trust and the Brookings Institution; he chairs Morehouse School of Medicine's board.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded 1989 and led as president and CEO.
Founding and managing partner of the D.C. strategy, policy and communications firm (2011).
Senior political strategist to Barack Obama's 2008 campaign.

legacyDetail.d: RLJ Lodging Trust, Brookings Institution, Meridian International Center.

humbleBeginnings: Trained as an accountant before turning to entertainment marketing.
breakthrough: Founded Liquid Soul in 2001, growing it into a full-service brand-marketing agency with offices in Atlanta, Washington, Los Angeles and Dallas.
legacy: Expanded into film producing alongside the agency's studio-marketing work.

Also credited as a film producer.

legacy: His 2026 "Possibility in Action" endowment drew matching pledges from Mielle founders Melvin and Monique Rodriguez and TIAA CEO Thasunda Brown Duckett.

breakthrough: After a 2015 Shark Tank rejection, she cold-pitched a Target buyer on LinkedIn and landed national distribution.
legacy: Moved The Lip Bar back to Detroit; by 2018 it was stocked in several hundred Target stores.

Reached Target via LinkedIn; in several hundred stores by 2018.

humbleBeginnings: Born in Washington, D.C.; worked as a steering-systems engineer at General Motors while earning her MBA.
breakthrough: Moved to Oregon in 2002 to help run her mother-in-law's McDonald's franchise; she and her husband now own several Portland-area McDonald's restaurants.
legacy: Parlayed her small-business profile into the Oregon House (2017–2025), where she chaired the economic development and small business committee, and Congress (2025–).

breakthrough: Inherited The Miami Times in 1970 and was its publisher until 1994, building it into Miami's leading Black newspaper.
legacy: Invested the paper's profits in bank stock and real estate, including a 5% stake in Bayside Marketplace; joined the Greater Miami Chamber in 1968 and the business elite's "Non-Group."

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran The Miami Times, founded by his father in 1923.

name: James A. Dallas Sr.
hbcuStory: Graduated from Florida A&M in 1942, where he played trombone in the university bands.
humbleBeginnings: An educator in segregated Fort Lauderdale who built businesses on the side.
breakthrough: Owned O'Dell's Lounge and Grill and The Big Savoy, nightclubs that served Black and white patrons during segregation, plus a grocery store and a pest-control company.
legacy: A civic power broker who helped recruit Black professionals to Fort Lauderdale and advised Alcee Hastings; the city named its first downtown street for an African American man after him.

hbcuStory: Graduated magna cum laude from Florida A&M University, where he was the first student speaker in the School of Business and Industry Forum series; inducted into the SBI Hall of Fame (2009).
humbleBeginnings: Came up through magazine publishing in New York.
breakthrough: Was founding president and CEO of VIBE Ventures from its 1993 launch, then chairman and CEO of Vanguard Media.
legacy: Later became a senior vice president of content development at ESPN.

name: Arthur J. Hill
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. from Florida Memorial College in 1971, then an M.A. in agricultural economics from the University of Florida (1973).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Jacksonville, one of four children of a single mother who worked as a beautician.
breakthrough: After a decade in corporate lending at Southeast Bank and AmeriFirst, became chairman, president and CEO of Miami's Peoples National Bank of Commerce (1984–1989), recapitalizing the distressed institution.
legacy: Named president of Ginnie Mae in 1989–90 and then HUD assistant secretary for housing under George H. W. Bush.

breakthroughDetail.d: Chairman, president and CEO, 1984–1989.
Confirmed by the Senate in 1990.

legacyDetail.d: HUD assistant secretary for housing through the end of the Bush administration.

name: Amy Surginer Northrop
hbcuStory: Earned a bachelor's degree in business at Allen University, then studied at the Manhattan Trade School.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Dixiana, South Carolina; worked in beauty shops in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New York.
breakthrough: Returned to Columbia in 1935 to open Amy's Beauty Shop and built the state's Black cosmetology associations.
legacy: Became South Carolina's first African American state inspector of beauty shops and a civic leader in Columbia.

breakthroughDetail.d: Opened in Columbia in 1935.
Hosted the first S.C. State Cosmetology Association clinic (1936); charter member of the Columbia Citywide Cosmetology Association (1938).

legacyDetail.d: First African American state inspector of beauty shops in South Carolina.

sources.label: South Carolina African American History Calendar — Amy Surginer Northrop

name: Bill Lucas
hbcuStory: A graduate of Florida A&M University.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Jacksonville, Florida; signed with the Milwaukee Braves as an infielder in 1957 and played six minor-league seasons.
breakthrough: Joined the Braves front office in 1965, became farm director, and in September 1976 was named the first African American general manager in Major League Baseball.
legacy: Hired Bobby Cox as manager in 1978; died in 1979 at 43 and is in the Braves Hall of Fame (2006).

breakthroughDetail.d: Named Braves general manager in September 1976.

legacyDetail.d: Inducted in 2006.
